description: Install Usage, write a CLI spec, and generate your first completions and documentation.
---

# Get started

This guide takes a small CLI definition through validation, completion, and
documentation generation. You only need the `usage` executable to try it.

Already using a CLI framework? [Export a spec with an integration](/spec/integrations).
Writing a script? [Start with the script guide](/cli/scripts).

## 1. Install Usage

Choose one command, then check that `usage` is on your `PATH`:

::: code-group

```sh [mise]
mise use -g usage
usage --version
```

```sh [Homebrew]
brew install usage
usage --version
```

```sh [Cargo]
cargo install usage-cli --locked
usage --version
```

:::

See [installation](/cli/) for prebuilt binaries and other package managers.

## 2. Describe your CLI

Save this as `ship.usage.kdl`:

```kdl
name "Ship"
bin "ship"
about "Deploy services from your terminal"

cmd "deploy" help="Deploy a service" {
    arg "<service>" help="Service to deploy"
    flag "-e --env <env>" help="Target environment" default="staging" {
        choices "staging" "production"
    }
}
```

This describes `ship deploy <service> --env <env>`. The service is required;
the environment defaults to `staging` and accepts either listed choice.

Usage specs use [KDL](https://kdl.dev/): each line is a node, properties use
`key=value`, and braces contain child nodes. See [spec basics](/spec/) for
booleans, optional arguments, and nested commands.

::: info A spec describes an interface
This file does not implement or install a `ship` command. Your application still
performs the deployment. Usage supplies the completions, documentation, and other
artifacts around that interface.
:::

## 3. Validate and try completion

Check the spec:

```sh
usage lint ship.usage.kdl
```

Ask Usage for completion candidates directly, without installing `ship`:

```sh
usage complete-word --file ship.usage.kdl -- ship deploy api --env prod
```

The result is `production`. Completion choices come from the same spec that will
supply your reference docs.

To enable Bash completion for an existing executable named `ship`:

```bash
usage generate completion bash ship --file ship.usage.kdl \
  --include-bash-completion-lib > ship.bash
source ./ship.bash
```

Type `ship deploy api --env ` and press Tab. The
[completion guide](/cli/completions) covers persistent setup, the other four
shells, and specs exported by a command.

## 4. Generate documentation

```sh
usage generate markdown --file ship.usage.kdl --out-file ship.md
usage generate manpage --file ship.usage.kdl --out-file ship.1
```

Open `ship.md` to see the command, argument, flag, choices, and default. Preview
the man page with `man ./ship.1`.

Regenerate these files whenever the CLI definition changes. Usage does not watch
your source files automatically; add generation to your build or release process.

## Where to go next

- [Shell completions](/cli/completions): install completions for your shell.
- [Scripts](/cli/scripts): let Usage parse arguments before your script runs.
- [Markdown](/cli/markdown): generate one page per command for a docs website.
- [SDKs](/cli/sdk): call your CLI from TypeScript or Python.
- [Spec reference](/spec/reference/): look up supported nodes and properties.
''',

description: Learn the KDL syntax for Usage commands, arguments, flags, defaults, and completion choices.
---

# Spec basics

A Usage spec describes a command-line interface: its commands, arguments, flags,
help text, and completion choices. Keep it in a `.usage.kdl` file,
[embed it in a script](/cli/scripts), or
[generate it from a CLI framework](/spec/integrations).

For a complete walkthrough, [start here](/guide/getting-started).

## Read the syntax

Specs use [KDL](https://kdl.dev/). A node starts with a name such as `arg` or
`flag`, followed by values and optional `key=value` properties. Braces hold
child nodes. Comments start with `//`.

```kdl
name "My CLI"
bin "mycli"
about "Manage local projects"

flag "-v --verbose" help="Enable verbose logging" global=#true
arg "[dir]" help="Project directory" default="."
```

Use KDL v2 booleans, `#true` and `#false`. Quote strings in examples and use
semicolons to separate nodes written on the same line:

```kdl
flag "--shell <shell>" { choices "bash" "zsh" "fish"; }
```

## Arguments and flags

| Syntax | Meaning | Example invocation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `arg "<file>"` | Required positional argument | `mycli report.txt` |
| `arg "[file]"` | Optional positional argument | `mycli` |
| `arg "<files>..."` | One or more positional values | `mycli a.txt b.txt` |
| `flag "-f --force"` | Boolean flag with a short alias | `mycli -f` |
| `flag "--output <file>"` | Flag that takes a value | `mycli --output out.txt` |
| `flag "--tag <tag>" var=#true` | Repeatable flag | `mycli --tag a --tag b` |

Give arguments and flags useful `help` text. It appears in generated documentation
and, when Usage parses a script, in its help output.

## Commands and global flags

Nest `cmd` nodes to describe subcommands. A flag with `global=#true` is also
available to descendant commands.

```kdl
bin "mycli"
flag "-v --verbose" help="Enable verbose logging" global=#true count=#true

cmd "config" help="Manage settings" subcommand_required=#true {
    cmd "set" help="Set a value" {
        arg "<key>" help="Setting name"
        arg "<value>" help="New value"
    }
    cmd "remove" help="Remove a value" {
        alias "rm"
        arg "<key>" help="Setting name"
    }
}
```

This describes `mycli config set <key> <value>` and `mycli config remove <key>`.
See the [command reference](/spec/reference/cmd) for aliases, examples, and
dynamic commands.

## Defaults and environment variables

When Usage parses arguments, an explicit command-line value takes priority over
an environment variable, which takes priority over a default. The order of
properties in the spec does not change that precedence.

```kdl
flag "-u --user <user>" help="User to run as" env="MYCLI_USER" default="admin"
```

Configuration metadata is a separate feature. It does not make the parser load
configuration files; see [configuration and defaults](/spec/reference/config).

## Completion choices

Use `choices` for a fixed list and `complete` for values supplied by a command:

```kdl
flag "--env <env>" help="Target environment" {
    choices "staging" "production"
}
arg "<service>" help="Service to deploy"
complete "service" run="mycli services list"
```

Usage validates `choices` when it parses a script. For an existing application,
its own argument parser remains responsible for validation.

## Validate a spec

```sh
usage lint mycli.usage.kdl
```

The linter reports parsing errors and common problems such as duplicate flags or
misplaced variadic arguments. Use `--warnings-as-errors` in CI to fail on warnings.

Continue to the [full spec reference](/spec/reference/) or
[generate shell completions](/cli/completions).
''',

description: Generate a single Markdown reference or one page per command from a Usage spec.
---

# Generate Markdown

Generate reference documentation from your command descriptions, arguments,
flags, choices, defaults, and examples.

## One file

```sh
usage generate markdown --file mycli.usage.kdl --out-file reference.md
```

The output includes the root command and its subcommands. Usage writes the whole
file, so keep handwritten introductions and tutorials in separate files.

## One page per command

```sh
usage generate markdown --file mycli.usage.kdl --multi \
  --out-dir docs/commands --url-prefix /commands
```

For a CLI with `config set` and `config remove` commands, the output includes:

```text
docs/commands/
├── index.md
├── config.md
└── config/
    ├── remove.md
    └── set.md
```

`--url-prefix` sets the base URL for links between generated command pages. Match
it to where the pages will be served on your website. Regeneration writes current
pages but does not remove files for commands you have deleted; clean the generated
directory when removing or renaming commands.

## Read a spec from another command

Use `--file -` to read standard input:

```sh
mycli --usage-spec | usage generate markdown --file - --out-file reference.md
```

The exporting command must print only the spec to standard output. Write log
messages to standard error.

## Format help and examples

- Use `help` for a short description and `long_help` for details.
- Use `help_md` when the Markdown description should differ from terminal help.
- Add [`example` nodes](/spec/reference/#examples) for common invocations.
- Set [`source_code_link_template`](/spec/reference/#source-code-links) to link
  commands to their implementation.
- Pass `--replace-pre-with-code-fences` to convert HTML `<pre>` blocks to Markdown
  fences, or `--html-encode` to escape HTML in help text.

## Keep generated docs current

Run the generation command as part of your build or release process. Commit the
output if your documentation host builds from checked-in Markdown, and review the
diff alongside the CLI change.

For all options, see [`usage generate markdown`](/cli/reference/generate/markdown).
''',

description: Generate, preview, and install Unix man pages from a Usage spec.
---

# Generate man pages

Usage generates Unix man pages in roff format from a spec's help text, commands,
arguments, flags, and examples.

## Generate and preview

```sh
usage generate manpage --file mycli.usage.kdl --out-file mycli.1
man ./mycli.1
```

Omit `--out-file` to write to standard output. To read a spec from a CLI:

```sh
mycli --usage-spec | usage generate manpage --file - --out-file mycli.1
```

## Choose a manual section

The default section is `1`, for user commands. Use `--section` and a matching file
extension when generating a different kind of manual:

```sh
usage generate manpage --file myconfig.usage.kdl --section 5 --out-file myconfig.5
```

| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | User commands |
| 5 | File formats and conventions |
| 7 | Miscellaneous documentation |
| 8 | System administration commands |

## Install a page

For a local installation on systems that search `~/.local/share/man`:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.local/share/man/man1
cp mycli.1 ~/.local/share/man/man1/
man mycli
```

Manual search paths vary by system. If `man mycli` does not find the page, use
`man ./mycli.1` to preview it, or install it in a directory on your system's manual
search path. Packaged CLIs should install the page through their package manager.

## Improve the generated content

Set top-level `about`, `long_about`, `author`, and `license` metadata, describe each
command and option, and add [`example` nodes](/spec/reference/#examples) for common
workflows. Regenerate the page when the interface changes.

For all options, see [`usage generate manpage`](/cli/reference/generate/manpage).
